newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-LOS ANGELES DODGERS UP FOR SALE.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-LOS ANGELES DODGERS UP FOR SALE.

text.p: The Los Angeles Dodgers, one of America's most famous and successful baseball teams, is up for sale, club president Peter O'Malley announced Monday.
"The time is right to sell," O'Malley told a news conference at Dodger Stadium.

The family-owned club -- the first big league team to set up shop on the West Coast when Walter O'Malley moved them to Los Angeles from Brooklyn in 1957 -- could fetch one of the highest purchase prices ever for a sports franchise.
"The time is approaching when a family can not support a major league baseball team. It is the time of corporate ownership," Peter O'Malley said. "All economic factors figure into this.
"Family ownership is probably a dying breed."
The team owns Dodger Stadium and the land around it in the heart of Los Angeles, as well as a training facility in Vero Beach, Florida, and a baseball camp in the Dominican Republic.
"I have no idea what the ballclub is worth," said O'Malley. "There is no price placed on it, but it is up for sale."
O'Malley said the club was not talking with anyone at the moment about a sale.
"There is no dialogue between us and prospective buyers," he told reporters, adding that he had received several offers over the last 30 years, but none ever went beyond the inquiry stage.
"The number one priority for our family is to identify good ownership for the Los Angeles Dodgers and for L.A."
O'Malley said there was no rush to sell the team, but suggested that five or six months would be a realistic period to complete the sale.

The club, which has won nine National League pennants and five World Series titles since moving from Brooklyn, New York, at the end of the 1957 season, has been owned by the O'Malley family for 47 years.

Peter O'Malley has served as president of the Dodgers since 1970 after replacing his father, Walter, who gained control of the Dodgers in 1950 and moved the franchise to Los Angeles, earning the lasting ire of Brooklyn baseball fans.
The team, which has a reputation for developing major league stars, has finished first or second 19 times in the National League West in the past 27 seasons.
The 1996 season was the 24th straight year that the team averaged more than two million fans. The Dodgers have passed the three million mark in attendance 11 times in Los Angeles, including 1996.
